extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, worldbuilders, and writers interested in designing magic systems (novice to experienced)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and evaluating fantasy magic systems (hard and soft) that serve story, character, and worldbuilding rather than acting as mere decoration. Emphasizes rules vs. mystery, the primacy of limitations, and strategies for deepening a system without needless complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's First Law: Understanding Equals Magic
rubrics_metrics.description: The more the reader understands how a magic system works, the more they can engage with it as a tool in the story; understanding enables the use of magic for problem-solving and plot mechanics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place your system on a spectrum from soft to hard depending on desired effect. This law is fundamental to choosing whether clarity or mystery will best serve your narrative; it applies beyond fantasy and to story design generally. Example framing: Hard systems allow strategic problem-solving; soft systems preserve wonder. Note Sanderson's caveat: these are observations about what improves his own systems, not absolute commandments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft Magic Systems — preserve wonder and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft magic deliberately keeps rules obscure to create a sense of wonder and to maintain narrative mystery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key characteristics: maintain a sense of wonder; create narrative tension through uncertainty; use magic to complicate rather than solve problems. Example: Tolkien — readers rarely understand capabilities of wizards on the page, which preserves the 'fish-out-of-water' feeling for protagonists. Anti-pattern: explaining or systematizing everything in a story where mystery is the point will reduce wonder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard Magic Systems — clear, understandable rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard magic systems provide explicit, consistent rules that readers can understand and anticipate, enabling satisfying, strategic uses of magic in plot resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard systems often draw on real-world analogues or internal logical systems; clarity allows readers to predict consequences and enjoy problem-solving (example: Spider-Man's defined powers). Use hard systems when you want cause-and-effect storytelling where magic functions like a technology or tool. Anti-pattern: vague rules in a system presented as hard will frustrate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's Second Law: Limitations > Powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on what magic cannot do (limitations) rather than cataloguing what it can do; constraints are more interesting than abilities themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design limitations that create narrative opportunity. The law reframes magic design from asking 'what can it do?' to 'what can't it do?' and 'what does it cost?' Example contrast: Superman is made interesting by his ethical code and kryptonite vulnerability. Treat limitations as primary drivers of conflict, stakes, and character growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Magical Limitations: limits, weaknesses, costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between fundamental constraints (limitations), exploitable vulnerabilities (weaknesses), and negative consequences of use (costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to craft varied and narratively rich constraints. Example: In The Wheel of Time, male channelers go insane (a cost) that creates long-term tension. When designing, specify which type a given constraint is and how it affects characters, plot, and worldbuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: What makes an excellent limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: An excellent limitation forces characters to work harder, increases narrative tension, and adds depth to worldbuilding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate limitations by whether they produce meaningful choices, raise stakes, and integrate with character arcs and society. Anti-patterns: limitations that exist only to prevent plot solutions without meaningful consequences or thematic fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's Third Law: Expand, Don't Add
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer expanding the implications of existing rules rather than adding more discrete powers; depth of exploration beats breadth of abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'worldbuilder's disease'—creating many powers with little depth. A smaller set of well-considered powers explored thoroughly will usually be more compelling than a thousand distinct abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy — Extrapolate: explore broader implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Take existing magical abilities and extrapolate their wider consequences for society, economics, culture, and daily life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'What happens when...?' and follow logical consequences across social institutions. Use extrapolation to create surprising but coherent worldbuilding details that feel earned rather than tacked on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy — Interconnect: tie magic to theme and story
rubrics_metrics.description: Interconnect magical mechanics with the story's themes, characters, and cultural systems so magic serves the narrative core.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect powers thematically and ensure magical elements contribute to character arcs and the story's central conflicts. Anti-pattern: magic as isolated gimmick that doesn't affect or reflect the story's themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy — Streamline: consolidate and avoid unnecessary complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce redundant magical concepts by consolidating and combining elements rather than continually adding new ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streamlining keeps the system comprehensible and focused; combine similar mechanics and remove elements that don't deepen the story. Anti-pattern: piling on powers for the sake of novelty without narrative purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical underpinnings of the laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws are broader narrative principles: limitations make characters more compelling; depth matters more than breadth; understanding systemic constraints creates more engaging narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the laws as storytelling tools applicable beyond magic — e.g., in technology, social systems, or other speculative elements. Use these philosophical points to evaluate whether a system deepens character and story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice for implementing magic systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete, actionable recommendations for writers implementing a magic system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include: determine the emotional core of your magical system; create clear internal logic; avoid using magic as a convenient plot device; make characters work within their magical constraints; consider the broader implications of magical abilities. Use these as a checklist when revising or designing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and limits of Sanderson's laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanderson's laws are guidelines, not absolute rules; they reflect what tends to make systems work well for the author and many readers but may be broken intentionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply laws judiciously—recognize when breaking a law could better serve tone, theme, or genre. The goal is to use magic to serve story, illuminate characters, and create meaningful tension rather than to follow rules for their own sake.
